title: The climate card China has yet to play
gist: Ober and Goh argue that as the US withdraws from climate institutions and closes visa pathways for Pacific Islanders, China has the money, technology (sponge cities, weather satellites) and relocation experience (9.6 million people relocated 2015–20) to make climate mobility a geopolitical lever — potentially centring it at COP33 in 2028 if it wins the hosting bid.

themes.theme: Pacific climate mobility as geopolitical bargaining chip

insights.claim: In 2025 the Pacific Islands Forum endorsed an implementation plan for its Pacific Regional Framework on Climate Mobility, including a Climate Mobility Action Hub, while Vanuatu and Fiji are building planned relocation into national policy.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Climate mobility is now institutionalised Pacific policy — a channel for great-power influence.

insights.claim: Australia's migration-pathway deal with Tuvalu gives Canberra a say in Tuvalu's defence agreements with third countries, showing climate mobility is becoming part of the security bargain.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Template for migration-for-security trades that shape Pacific basing and alignment.

insights.claim: Under the Compact of Free Association, Marshall Islands and Palau citizens — among Taiwan's remaining partners — can move freely to the US in exchange for US defence rights, while Solomon Islands, Kiribati (2019) and Nauru (2024) switched recognition from Taiwan to China.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Mobility access underpins US defence posture in the Pacific; erosion could shift recognition battles.

themes.theme: US retreat from climate policy and Pacific visas

insights.claim: In January 2026 the Trump administration announced US withdrawal from the UNFCCC and the IPCC, having already left the Green Climate Fund the year before.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: US absence from climate governance opens leadership vacuum China can fill.

insights.claim: The Biden-era climate-migration agenda (first US government report, interagency working group, near-launched Climate Mobility Plan of Action) has been reversed.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Policy whiplash reduces US credibility with Pacific partners.
insights.quote: That work has now been reversed.

insights.claim: Tuvalu, Tonga and Vanuatu appeared on a State Department visa-restriction list and Fiji was caught in a January 2026 immigrant-visa suspension, meaning the US is closing pathways Pacific states rely on as an adaptation strategy.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: US visa closures are a self-inflicted loss of influence in a contested region.

themes.theme: China's climate-mobility toolkit and COP33 opportunity

insights.claim: COP33 in 2028 will be hosted by an Asia-Pacific country, India has withdrawn, and China is reportedly weighing a bid; the summit would likely open days after the next US presidential election.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: A Chinese COP33 presidency would amplify China's green-tech and climate-finance soft power.

insights.claim: The authors suggest China could do something no COP presidency has done: put climate mobility at the centre of the summit, bundling Climate Mobility Action Hub funding, adaptation expertise and relocation planning.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Watch China's COP33 bid and any Pacific mobility packages as indicators of influence push.
insights.quote: put climate mobility at the centre of the summit

insights.claim: In May 2025 Beijing pledged $2 million for Pacific climate cooperation and 100 'small and beautiful' community projects over three years, plus early-warning and coastal-protection collaboration using its weather satellites.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Small-dollar but high-visibility Chinese projects build influence cheaply.

insights.claim: China relocated 9.6 million people between 2015 and 2020, including many from disaster-prone areas, and has built 'sponge cities' with measurable flood-resilience gains — relocation scale and speed no other country matches.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: China's resilience tech and know-how are exportable — a soft-power and contractor-export opportunity.

insights.claim: A bolder Chinese move would be opening temporary labour pathways for its most climate-exposed partners as Washington shrinks visa access.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Would be a significant shift in Pacific alignment dynamics.

themes.theme: Constraints on Beijing and middle-power competition

insights.claim: Beijing may hesitate because elevating its relocation record would invite scrutiny of documented human rights concerns and community consent, and it prefers helping countries keep people in place, backing Pacific statehood claims.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Base case may be China sticking to seawalls and satellites rather than explicit mobility agenda.

insights.claim: New Zealand committed NZ$17.9 million (about US$10 million) in August to a Pacific Climate Mobility Partnerships Program, but no middle power can match China's money, technology and relocation experience.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Middle powers like Australia/NZ can't fully fill the US gap.
insights.quote: no middle power can match China’s money, technology, and relocation experience

insights.claim: Pacific Island states hold a dozen UN seats and carry real weight in consensus-based climate negotiations, making them valuable diplomatic partners for China.
insights.speaker: Kayly Ober
insights.so_what: Pacific vote bloc matters in UN/climate outcomes that affect carbon markets and climate finance.
